Traditional · The Seoul Table

Doenjang Jjigae

A comforting Korean stew that gives fermented soybean paste its own place at the table.

Korean · Easy · Serves 3–4 (one pot)

Jump to recipe ↓

Behind the dish

Lane: traditional — the paste's big sister, and the pot this site owes respect to. Straight talk: doenjang jjigae uses no gochujang at all. It is the soybean paste's own stew — the deeper, funkier, older sibling in the jang family — and it is on this site because the paste's story is incomplete without it: same ancestry, same beans, different fork. This is the everyday pot of the Korean home, twenty minutes from pantry to table, and the record where this opinionated site goes quiet with respect. Heat dial: 1 — a pinch of gochugaru's warmth, nothing more.

Set yourself up

Before you cook

  • The anchovy-kelp stock is the pot's quiet excellence — ten minutes of simmering the two in the water, then straining. Water works; the stock turns the same pot from good to the thing you crave on a cold Tuesday. Make it while everything else gets cut.
  • Dissolve the doenjang in a ladle of the hot stock before it joins the pot — paste dropped into the broth in lumps stays in lumps; the ladle-dissolve is the one-move technique.

Let’s make it.

  1. 01
    The dissolved paste, the gochugaru, and the optional gochujang into the simmering stock; the potato, onion, and zucchini in; 8 minutes at a steady bubble — the root vegetables need the head start. Checkpoint — the broth has gone from clear to cloudy-gold, and the smell is the ferment's deep, savory, slightly funky register — the smell this site's other pages orbit around. Taste: saltier than drinking broth, correct for a rice-adjacent stew.
  2. 02
    The tofu, kimchi, and mushrooms in, 5 more minutes — the tofu warms through and the kimchi's sour edge dissolves into the broth's depth. Checkpoint — the potato is tender at a poke, the tofu hot to its center, and the broth tastes of the two ferments and the sea's stock — the kimchi's age determining its sour presence (young jar: a bright note; elder jar: the pot's backbone).
  3. 03
    Garlic, scallions, chilies, and the sesame oil finish over the top, pot off the heat, straight to the table in its own vessel. Checkpoint — the eating test with rice: a spoon of broth, a piece of tofu, a bite of rice — the broth's funk and depth should make the rice disappear at a pace that embarrasses the cook's plans for leftovers. If the broth tastes flat, it wants salt's carrier — another half-spoon of doenjang dissolved in the ladle, not table salt. Chef’s Note — the jjigae pot is where this site's single-paste thesis gets its honest footnote: the jang family is a household, and gochujang is its loudest member, not its only one. Doenjang runs deeper (longer fermentation, more soy, no chile), and the home table runs both pots in the same week — the chile stew for appetite, the soybean stew for comfort. A cook who owns the gochujang jar and not the doenjang tub knows only half the family's recipes.

Troubleshooting

SymptomCauseFix
Broth flatWater stock or shy pasteThe anchovy-kelp base; the half-spoon more
Paste in lumpsDropped in wholeThe ladle-dissolve, always
Tofu fell apartBoiled hard or soft tofuFirm tofu, steady bubble
Too saltyPaste over-run plus kimchi brineDilute with hot water; taste before the final spoon

Storage, Make-Ahead & Variations

  • Keeps 2 days and improves; the next day's reheated pot with fresh scallions over is the tradition's own day-after. (The dolsot's leftover components (#4) into this pot is the fridge's finest zero-waste move.)
  • Variations: the clam pot (a handful of the #SF15 clams in at step 2, their liquor the stock's upgrade); the beef-and-mushroom build; the full honesty pot with no gochujang at all — the tradition's own, and this site bows to it.
